blocks.text: Give an object its own thread and request queue, so callers invoke it asynchronously and get futures back.

Method calls become **requests** placed on a queue. A single **scheduler** thread takes them one at a time and runs them on a plain, unsynchronized **servant**. The caller gets a future immediately and never touches the servant's state.

items: **Concurrency control:** thread confinement, so the servant needs no locks.
**Caller experience:** an ordinary method that returns a future.
**Ordering:** requests run in the order they were enqueued.

blocks.text: The actor model is this idea scaled up: many active objects, each with a mailbox, communicating only by messages.

walkthrough.note: The servant is plain, single-threaded code. It has no locks and no `volatile`, because only one thread ever runs it.
The proxy turns a call into a request: a `Runnable` that completes a future. `enqueue` is the only way in, and the queue is the activation queue.
The scheduler thread takes requests in FIFO order and runs each. A poison pill stops it; `close` then joins the thread.
Calls return at once with futures. Results arrive in submission order: 1, 3, 6.
Four threads call concurrently, yet no total is lost. Each insertion into the queue happens-before its `take`, and only one thread touches the servant.

blocks.text: A device driver that allows only one command at a time.

A lab-automation service talks to a robotic arm over a serial line. The vendor library is not thread-safe and each command takes seconds. Many HTTP threads want to issue commands. A `RobotArm` active object queues every command, runs them one by one on its own thread, and hands each caller a future for the outcome.
Payoff: the unsafe driver is never shared, request threads never block on hardware, and command order is explicit.

lists.title: Use when
items: A non-thread-safe resource must be shared by many callers.
Callers should not block on slow work.
You want serialized access without lock reasoning.

lists.title: Avoid when
items: Calls are fast and a `synchronized` block or lock is simpler.
Callers need the result immediately on the same thread.

lists.title: Pitfalls
items: An unbounded queue hides overload and grows until memory runs out.
A request that blocks stalls every request behind it.
Never touch the servant from outside; one leaking reference breaks confinement.

lists.title: Overuse smells
items: One thread per tiny object, which wastes memory and context switches.
Futures that every caller immediately blocks on.

lists.title: Modern Java
items: `Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor()` plus `CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(task, executor)` is a compact active object.
A virtual thread draining a queue makes one active object per entity cheap.

rows.difference: Producer-consumer decouples any producers from any consumers through a queue. An active object is one consumer whose queue carries method requests and returns futures.
A pool runs tasks on any worker, so they may overlap. An active object funnels all requests for one servant through exactly one thread, giving mutual exclusion.
The future is how the active object returns results. The pattern adds the queue, the scheduler and the confinement of state.
The caller-facing object is a proxy, but it forwards through a queue to another thread instead of delegating directly.
Each queued request is a command object, here a `Runnable` closure, that the scheduler executes later.

entries.name: Actor / ActorRef
entries.detail: Each actor has a mailbox and processes one message at a time; `ask` returns a future, as in an active object.

entries.name: Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor
entries.detail: One thread plus an unbounded queue, with `CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(task, executor)` for the proxy side.

entries.name: HandlerThread and Handler
entries.detail: A looper thread drains a message queue; posted work runs serially on that thread.

entries.name: SwingUtilities.invokeLater
entries.detail: Requests are queued to the single event dispatch thread, which owns all UI state.

options.why: State is confined to one thread; method calls become queued requests that return futures.
A pool spreads independent tasks across workers. Here one thread owns the state, so the calls are serialized on purpose.
Futures are returned, but the defining feature is the single owning thread and request queue.
A proxy would delegate on the caller's thread; this hands the work to another thread.

exercises.scenario: A vendor SDK for a label printer is not thread-safe and each print takes about 300 ms. Forty request threads need to print labels. They should not block, and prints must happen one at a time in arrival order.

options.why: One owning thread runs queued requests in order, and callers receive futures instead of waiting.
Every print is a write, so callers would still queue up and block, and the lock gives no ordering guarantee.
A pool runs tasks in parallel, which would call the unsafe SDK from several threads at once.
Immutability removes shared mutable state; the printer is inherently stateful and cannot be made immutable.

exercises.prompt: Explain Active Object in your own words: how does it avoid locks, and how does it differ from a thread pool?

modelAnswer.text: An active object owns one thread and a queue. Calls become requests on the queue and return futures, and the scheduler thread runs them one at a time on a plain servant. Because only that thread touches the state, no locks are needed. A thread pool instead runs unrelated tasks in parallel on any worker.

keyPoints: Calls become queued requests, executed by one thread
Callers get futures and do not block
State is confined to the scheduler thread, so no locks
A pool shares tasks across threads; an active object serializes one servant
